ideas.title: Overlay Exit Check for Small Shopify Shops

notes.stateful: Each store keeps a dated history of runs and a fix log, so the owner can show when each problem was found and when it was fixed.
notes.connected: Walks the merchant's live storefront, authorised by a Shopify crawler access key the merchant creates in their own admin, which also proves they control the store.
notes.unattended: A weekly scheduled re-run of the buying path emails the owner and their developer when a step changes.
notes.engine: A journey runner that drives home, product, cart and checkout entry by keyboard, captures what a screen reader is given at each step, detects the overlay, and runs the path twice: overlay blocked, and overlay with its own screen-reader mode switched on.
notes.shared: The owner sends a read-only, revocable report link to the shop's developer, who works through the findings.

buildPlan.title: One store, one walk
buildPlan.delivers: Sign in, add a store you control (verified by a crawler access key or a theme meta tag), and get a deployed report of a keyboard walk from the home page to checkout entry with what a screen reader is told at each step.
buildPlan.acceptance: On a test store the owner controls, the walk reaches checkout entry and the deployed report shows each step's announcement; an unverified store URL is refused.

buildPlan.title: Overlay blocked and overlay switched on
buildPlan.delivers: Detect the installed overlay, re-run the walk with its script blocked, and again with its screen-reader mode switched on, and show the three runs side by side per step.
buildPlan.acceptance: On the test store with a free overlay plan installed, all three runs complete and the per-step differences appear; the 'on' run shows the overlay's screen-reader mode as active.

buildPlan.title: Works across themes
buildPlan.delivers: Selectors by role and name, cart drawer or cart page, variant pickers, popups recorded as findings, and the crawler-key header on every request.
buildPlan.acceptance: The walk reaches checkout entry on at least 4 of 5 free Shopify themes; a run stopped by bot protection is labelled 'stopped at step N', with a screenshot.

buildPlan.title: Findings the developer can act on
buildPlan.delivers: Findings in plain words with the step, the element, the WCAG reference and a screenshot; PDF and CSV export; a revocable share link.
buildPlan.acceptance: The export lists every failed step; the share link opens signed out and stops working once revoked.

buildPlan.title: Fix log and weekly re-run
buildPlan.delivers: Mark items fixed with a note, a scheduled weekly re-run, and an email when results change.
buildPlan.acceptance: A fixed item clears on the next run and the log shows the found and fixed dates; a seeded change sends exactly one email.

buildPlan.title: Payment and polish
buildPlan.delivers: A one-off report and a monthly plan, owner README, phone layout, the app's own accessibility checked with Screen Reader Journeys, claims wording ('not an audit, not legal advice'), walkthrough test.
buildPlan.acceptance: A new account buys and receives a report end to end; axe reports no serious issues; no page claims compliance or protection.

ideas.summary: For small Shopify shops running an accessibility overlay: walks the buying path by keyboard with a screen reader's view, with the overlay blocked and with it switched on, and gives the shop's developer a dated findings list and a fix log before the owner decides whether to remove it.

public.summary: Find out whether a blind customer can actually get from your home page to checkout, with and without your accessibility widget.
public.problem: You installed an accessibility widget because you were told it would protect you, but shops with widgets still get demand letters, and some widgets slow the site down. You have no way to see what a screen-reader user meets on the way to checkout, or what changes if you take the widget off.
public.forWhom: Owners of small Shopify shops who run an accessibility widget or have received an accessibility complaint.
benefits: See every step of your buying path the way a screen-reader user meets it
Know what your widget changes before you keep or remove it
Hand your developer a clear, dated list of what to fix
Keep a record of what was fixed and when
Hear about it when a theme or app update breaks the path again

ideas.problemStatement: Small Shopify merchants installed accessibility overlays to avoid lawsuits and were sued anyway: one installed accessiBe after a lawsuit and was 'hit with a second lawsuit soon after' for 'minor bugs' the widget did not catch; another says the overlay slowed the site and the vendor 'continues to misrepresent the legal coverage'; a UserWay customer paying $1,300 a year is in a lawsuit. They cannot see whether a screen-reader user can reach checkout, or what removing the widget would change.
ideas.description: The owner adds their store and proves control with a Shopify crawler access key (or a theme meta tag). A worker on the backend, built on the engine of the owner's Screen Reader Journeys, walks home, a product page, add to cart, cart and checkout entry by keyboard and records what a screen reader is given at each step. It detects the installed overlay and runs the path twice more: with the overlay's script blocked, and with the overlay's own screen-reader mode switched on (accessiBe, for example, does not detect screen readers and needs Alt+1). The report lists failures in plain words with the step, the element, the WCAG reference and a screenshot, for the shop's developer; the owner marks fixes, and a weekly re-run updates the dated log. It makes no compliance or legal claim and is not an audit.
ideas.targetCustomer: Owners of small US-facing Shopify stores who run an accessibility overlay (accessiBe, UserWay, Accessibly and similar) or who have received an accessibility demand letter, and the developer who looks after their theme.
ideas.buyer: The store owner, on a personal or business card: a $49 one-off report, or $19 a month for re-runs and the fix log, against $49 to $349 a month for UserWay plans.
ideas.whyNow: The FTC's final order of 2025-04-22 bars accessiBe from claiming its automated products make a site WCAG-compliant; UsableNet's 2026 report (updated 2026-11-25) says widgets 'do not materially reduce legal risk' and counts 95 to 155 suits a month against companies using them; merchants posted in July and September 2026 that they were sued despite a widget; and Shopify's crawler access keys (2025-08-29) let a merchant authorise their own testing tool past bot protection.
ideas.founderFit: He ships web apps alone in days, and his own Screen Reader Journeys project already runs scripted screen-reader journeys through web apps, which is the engine this needs.

ideas.techStack: React + Vite front end, Supabase sign-in and per-app schema, the Screen Reader Journeys worker (headless browser) on Render, Resend for email, a hosted payment link.

pricing.model: One-off report plus an optional monthly plan
pricing.pricePoint: $49 one-off exit report; $19 a month for weekly re-runs, the fix log and the share link
pricing.rationale: Below UserWay's $49 to $349 a month and close to the $5 to $29 a month page scanners, justified by the journey and the overlay comparison; it is a report for a developer, not the audit a lawyer asks for after a demand letter, which costs far more.

ideas.revenueSketch: Estimate: 500 ad visitors a month converting at 2% gives 10 reports a month ($490); if 30% keep the $19 plan, about 18 subscribers ($340 a month) after six months. Unvalidated.
ideas.distribution: Search ads on overlay-removal and widget-lawsuit queries to a landing page first. The Shopify App Store comes later and needs an embedded app: its rules say 'Apps that don't use or need any Shopify APIs are not permitted' (2.2.1), apps 'must use Shopify App Pricing or the Shopify Billing API for all app charges' (1.2), and 'Don't use stats, data, or unsubstantiated claims such as guarantees in the listing' (4.3.3) (https://shopify.dev/docs/apps/launch/shopify-app-store/app-store-requirements). Shopify Community: rule unknown: check before posting (its FAQ returned 429). Google Ads: rule unknown: check before posting.

validationTest.method: A landing page ('See what your accessibility widget is hiding: a screen-reader walk to your checkout, with the widget off and on') with a refundable $49 pre-order button and a waitlist that asks for a store URL, driven by a $150, two-week Google search-ad test on overlay-removal and widget-lawsuit queries. No outreach, and no posting in any review thread. In parallel, a one-day spike that reaches checkout entry on 5 free themes with accessiBe's screen-reader mode switched on.
validationTest.successCriteria: From at least 400 visitors, at least 5 refundable pre-orders or 15 price-button clicks with 8 waitlist sign-ups giving a store URL; the spike reaches checkout entry on at least 4 of 5 themes.
validationTest.cost: About $150 in ads and two days of work.

ideas.moat: Weak to moderate: a library of Shopify theme and cart-drawer journeys, overlay signatures and their screen-reader-mode switches, each store's dated history, and the Screen Reader Journeys engine that page scanners lack.
compliance: Claims: no compliance, protection or legal-advice claims (FTC order against accessiBe; Shopify App Store requirement 4.3.3); label every report 'not an audit, not legal advice'.
Misuse: issue reports only for stores whose control is proven, since plaintiff firms already scan stores for widgets.
Accessibility: the app's own interface meets WCAG 2.2 AA.
Privacy (GDPR, UK GDPR): only merchant account data; synthetic data in checkout fields; no shopper data stored; crawler keys stored encrypted with an expiry.

risks.risk: Owners want legal protection, which a report cannot give, and money after a demand letter goes to lawyers and manual audits.
risks.mitigation: Sell it as the check before removing a widget and as a fix list for the developer; no badges; run the refundable pre-order test before building past milestone 1.

risks.risk: Themes, popups and bot protection break the walk, and each overlay switches on its screen-reader mode differently.
risks.mitigation: Crawler access keys, selectors by role and name, 'stopped at step N' recorded as a finding, and overlay support added one vendor at a time starting with the two largest.

risks.risk: The idea overlaps the published Popup Check (2026-11-03) for the same shops, and big vendors (BrowserStack) are adding screen-reader journeys.
risks.mitigation: Ship it as a vertical of Screen Reader Journeys that includes popups as findings, so Picker treats it as superseding Popup Check rather than shipping both.

scoreRationale.pain: Merchants on three overlay listings say they were sued despite the widget, one within 90 days (2026-09-18) and one within 180 (2026-07-16): https://apps.shopify.com/accesswidget/reviews?sort_by=newest and https://apps.shopify.com/userway-accessibility/reviews?ratings%5B%5D=1&ratings%5B%5D=2&sort_by=newest.
scoreRationale.willingnessToPay: Merchants pay $49 to $349 a month for overlays (https://apps.shopify.com/userway-accessibility), but that money buys 'protection', the listings are small (11 and 17 reviews), and paid page scanners for this job sell at $5 to $29 a month with 0 to 2 reviews (https://apps.shopify.com/accessifyai): 3, not 4.
scoreRationale.reachability: Owners are outside the owner's stated network; the self-serve channel is paid search, already crowded by vendor guides (https://testparty.ai/blog/ada-demand-letter-shopify-merchant-guide), and the App Store needs an embedded app.
scoreRationale.competitiveGap: No merchant-facing tool runs a buying-path screen-reader walk or compares the store with the overlay off and on, but page scanners are cheap (https://apps.shopify.com/accesskit) and BrowserStack's beta agent drives NVDA through tasks (https://www.browserstack.com/docs/accessibility/screen-reader-launcher/screen-reader-experience-agent).
scoreRationale.feasibility: The Screen Reader Journeys engine exists, but a walk that survives many themes, switching on each overlay's screen-reader mode (https://accessibe.com/blog/knowledgebase/screen-reader-guide) and proving store control (https://changelog.shopify.com/posts/authorize-custom-crawlers-and-tools-with-new-crawler-access-keys) fill the 7 days.
scoreRationale.complianceBurden: No regulated data; the burden is claims, after the FTC order (https://ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2025/04/ftc-approves-final-order-requiring-accessibe-pay-1-million), and refusing reports on stores the user does not control.

review.findings: Total 22 to 20, willingnessToPay 4 to 3 and feasibility 4 to 3. Confirmed the accessiBe, UserWay and Accessibly reviews and dates, UserWay's prices and Shopify's crawler access keys. Found cheaper page scanners than the researcher reported (AccessKit at $0 to $4.99, AccessifyAI at $4.99 to $14.99, Consentmo's bundled scanner), BrowserStack's beta Screen Reader Experience Agent driving real NVDA through tasks, and AudioEye's manual flow audits; no merchant-facing journey or overlay comparison exists. willingnessToPay 4 misread the rubric: the overlay listings have 11 and 17 reviews, the money bought 'protection', the $253 review is a refund dispute and was dropped, and after a demand letter merchants hire lawyers and manual audits ($2,000 to $8,500, a vendor guide). An 'overlay on' run must switch on the overlay's screen-reader mode, since accessiBe does not detect screen readers. Not a duplicate of Popup Check (2026-11-03), but this idea's findings include popups, so treat it as superseding it rather than shipping both. Added: proof of store control before any report, since plaintiff firms scan stores for widgets.

gateGap.closedBy: The refundable $49 pre-order in the validation test would show payment for this exact job and could raise willingnessToPay to 4; the theme spike with the overlay's screen-reader mode on would raise feasibility back to 4. Both together would take the total to 22.

ideas.title: Delivery Note Bill Check for Small Wholesalers

notes.stateful: Keeps a price book per supplier learned from accepted invoices, remembered line matches, a duplicate index and the list of credits still owed.
notes.unattended: A weekly digest of open credits and unresolved checks goes out from a scheduled job.
notes.engine: Aligns lines across the invoice, the delivery note and the order, and applies tolerance rules for quantity, unit of measure, unit price, tax rate and arithmetic, plus duplicate rules.
notes.shared: The person receiving goods logs short or damaged lines on a phone at the door, the admin checks the invoice, and the owner sees the credits owed.

buildPlan.title: One invoice, one delivery note
buildPlan.delivers: Sign in, create a business, upload a supplier invoice PDF and a delivery-note photo, and see a side-by-side table with quantity differences after line extraction through the LLM gateway.
buildPlan.acceptance: On 5 sample pairs the short-delivered lines show correctly at the live URL.

buildPlan.title: Matching engine
buildPlan.delivers: Line alignment by code and description with remembered manual matches per supplier; checks for quantity, unit of measure (cases against units), unit price, tax rate and totals; the purchase order as an optional third document; one invoice across several deliveries.
buildPlan.acceptance: 20 fixture documents with known discrepancies, including a unit-of-measure case, a substitution and a split delivery, are all flagged correctly; a manual re-match is remembered on the next invoice.

buildPlan.title: Price book and duplicates
buildPlan.delivers: The last accepted price per item per supplier, price-rise flags, and duplicate detection by supplier and invoice number and by amount and date.
buildPlan.acceptance: A re-uploaded invoice is flagged as a duplicate and a seeded price rise is flagged.

buildPlan.title: Receiving at the door
buildPlan.delivers: Owner, admin and receiver roles; phone capture of the delivery note; tap to record short or damaged lines.
buildPlan.acceptance: A shortage logged on a phone appears on the admin's check of the matching invoice.

buildPlan.title: Credits owed and export
buildPlan.delivers: Each discrepancy becomes a credit request with a status; a weekly digest email from a scheduled job; CSV export of checked rows for any accounting tool.
buildPlan.acceptance: The digest sends on schedule in test and the CSV imports into a Sheets template.

buildPlan.title: Usage caps
buildPlan.delivers: A monthly usage counter per business, an LLM spending cap, the visitor's-own-key option and a checkout link.
buildPlan.acceptance: The cap stops extraction past the limit with a clear message, and a test payment raises it.

buildPlan.title: Polish
buildPlan.delivers: Owner README, phone layout, keyboard and screen-reader pass, walkthrough test.
buildPlan.acceptance: A walkthrough test runs sign-in to credit export on a phone and a desktop; axe reports no serious issues.

ideas.summary: For small wholesalers and shops that pay someone to tick supplier invoices against delivery notes: checks each invoice against what arrived and the agreed price, flags short deliveries, price rises and duplicates, and keeps the list of credits still owed.

public.summary: Check every supplier invoice against what actually arrived, and keep track of the credits you are owed.
public.problem: Before you pay a supplier, someone sits with the invoice, the delivery note and your order and ticks every line. It takes hours every week, short deliveries and quiet price rises still slip through, and nobody chases the credits.
public.forWhom: Owners and office staff of small wholesalers, distributors and shops that receive goods against orders.
benefits: Short deliveries and price rises caught before you pay
A running list of credits your suppliers owe you
Shortages logged at the door, on a phone
Hours of paperwork checking back every week

ideas.problemStatement: Small businesses pay freelancers by the hour to check each supplier invoice against the matching purchase order or receipt and the delivery records before it is entered (two such jobs posted on 2026-11-21 and 2026-11-23), because their accounting tool links bills to orders but does not flag price or quantity differences, and short deliveries and credits owed are tracked by hand.
ideas.description: The admin uploads a supplier invoice (PDF or photo), the delivery note, and optionally the purchase order; the person receiving goods can photograph the delivery note at the door and tap any short or damaged lines. Lines are extracted through the LLM gateway, then a deterministic matching engine aligns them and checks quantity, unit of measure, unit price against the supplier's learned price book, tax and arithmetic, and duplicates. Every discrepancy becomes a credit request with a status, a weekly digest lists what is still owed, and checked rows export as CSV for whatever accounting tool the business uses. It does not create purchase orders, approve or pay bills, or write into an accounting system.
ideas.targetCustomer: Owners and office or admin staff at small wholesalers, distributors and independent shops (about 1 to 20 staff, tens to a few hundred supplier invoices a month) that receive goods against orders and are not on Shopify or Xero, whether they keep their books in a spreadsheet or in QuickBooks Online, Zoho or Odoo.
ideas.buyer: The owner, from the business's software budget, in place of an hourly freelancer or admin time: $29 a month up to about 150 invoices, $59 up to about 500.
ideas.whyNow: Businesses posted paid jobs for exactly this hand check on 2026-11-21 and 2026-11-23; vendors' own features stop at linking a bill to an order (QuickBooks Online Plus and Advanced, help article updated 2026-07-16; Xero from 2026-06-17) or compare quantities only (Odoo 19), and the tools that compare lines cost $100 a month (Nanonets) to $319 a month (Lightyear).

problemEvidence.summary: Pays INR 750 to 1,250 an hour for someone to check each PDF supplier invoice against its purchase order or receipt (supplier, date, totals), enter it in Google Sheets and flag mismatches for supplier follow-up.

ideas.distribution: Google search ads and a page with a free one-off check (one invoice and one delivery note, no sign-up, files deleted after 24 hours). validationTest.method: No outreach. The free one-off check page (upload an invoice and a delivery note, see the difference table) with a 'Start at $29 a month' button that opens a waitlist, driven by a 14-day Google search-ad test on queries such as 'check invoice against delivery note'. Over the same weeks, re-run the freelancer.com spend searches and count jobs for this check, reading each job's own page.

validationTest.cost: About $150 in ads, LLM use capped at $20, and one build day.

Accessibility: the app itself meets WCAG 2.2 AA.
Records: the app is not the system of record; the business's duty to keep accounting records stays with its accounting system.
No tax-software recognition needed: it files and issues nothing.

risks.mitigation: The receiver taps shortages at the door, and every flag shows both documents side by side for a person to confirm.

risks.risk: Demand is thin: two paid jobs whose independence is unknown and no complaint from the target customer.
risks.mitigation: Run the free-check and price-button test before building past milestone 1, and stop below the threshold.

risks.mitigation: Stay tool-agnostic and cheap, export only, and compete on the price book, the credits list and capture at the door.

scoreRationale.complianceBurden: Commercial documents only, with processor duties under GDPR and the LLM gateway as a subprocessor; no regulated data and nothing filed (https://www.freelancer.com/api/projects/0.1/projects/40830879/?full_description=true).

review.findings: competitiveGap 3 to 2 and total 18 to 17; Shopify retailers dropped from the scope. Confirmed both jobs (40828455, 2026-11-21; 40830879, 2026-11-23) as this check, written by in-house businesses, one of which already has an accounting system, so the customer is not only spreadsheet keepers; the other two gatherer jobs are not this task. ideas.title: Heard-As Check for Tagged PDFs

notes.stateful: Keeps each file's run history across file versions and pdf.js versions, so a team sees when a reading changed and why.
notes.connected: Runs as a step in the team's own CI with their API key and reports back on the pull request, alongside a web upload for one-off checks.
notes.unattended: A weekly scheduled re-run of saved files on the latest pdf.js emails the team when what a reader is given changes.
notes.engine: Turns the accessibility tree that pdf.js's tagged layer exposes into a speech-style transcript (roles, table size and headers, alt text, language changes), walks the structure tree for the intended reading, and diffs the two.

buildPlan.title: One PDF, one transcript
buildPlan.delivers: Upload a tagged PDF and get, from the backend's headless browser running the current pinned pdf.js, a raw transcript of what its tagged layer exposes, deployed.
buildPlan.acceptance: On the live URL a test file shows its heading, a 3-row table with headers and the figure's alt text; the pdf.js version is printed on the result.

buildPlan.title: Speech-style transcript
buildPlan.delivers: The raw tree becomes a transcript in the order and words a screen reader would use: role announcements, table size and headers, alt text, language changes.
buildPlan.acceptance: Five sample PDFs give stable expected transcripts across two runs.

buildPlan.title: Intended reading and diff
buildPlan.delivers: A structure-tree walker (order, ActualText, Alt, Lang) and a side-by-side diff that names each fault class.
buildPlan.acceptance: A reversed right-to-left line, untagged table-cell text and a missing alt text are each flagged on fixture files that pass veraPDF.

buildPlan.title: veraPDF beside it
buildPlan.delivers: veraPDF's PDF/UA results shown next to the diff, using the veraPDF service Tagging Doctor already runs, and a note when a fault is a known pdf.js viewer bug rather than the file's.
buildPlan.acceptance: A file that passes veraPDF but shows a heard-as fault is labelled 'passes validator, fails reading'; a constant viewer quirk is labelled as such and not counted against the file.

buildPlan.title: CI step and history
buildPlan.delivers: Sign-in, an API key, a sample GitHub Actions step that fails the build on new faults, per-file history, and a weekly re-run on the latest pdf.js with a change email.
buildPlan.acceptance: A seeded regression fails the sample workflow; a changed transcript sends exactly one email.

buildPlan.title: Polish
buildPlan.delivers: Developer README, retention setting for saved files, phone layout, the tool's own WCAG 2.2 AA pass checked with Screen Reader Journeys, walkthrough test.

public.summary: See what a screen reader will be given from your PDF, not just whether it passes a checker.
public.problem: Your tagged PDFs pass the validator, yet a listener can still hear a right-to-left line backwards, miss a table's cell text or get no description for a figure. Today you only find out by testing by hand, one viewer and one file at a time.

ideas.problemStatement: Tagged-PDF generators and remediators rely on validators that check structure, not what reaches a listener: a developer found that 'veraPDF's PDF/UA-1 check passes all three, but assistive technology reads the text wrong' (2026-11-22), and a tester found that VoiceOver says 'Table not found' on a valid tagged PDF/UA-1 table in Firefox's viewer while NVDA reads it (2026-11-25).
ideas.description: A developer uploads a tagged PDF or adds a step to their CI. A backend worker opens the file in a pinned version of pdf.js in headless Chromium, captures the accessibility tree its tagged layer exposes, and turns it into a speech-style transcript. A structure-tree walker builds the intended reading, and a diff names each fault class: reading order, untagged content, missing alt text, language changes, reversed right-to-left text, table size and headers. veraPDF's results sit beside it. It is a simulation from pdf.js in Chromium, labelled as such: it does not run Acrobat, Firefox's own accessibility layer or a real screen reader, and it cannot reproduce viewer bugs that depend on element size. It is best built as a PDF mode of Screen Reader Journeys, using Tagging Doctor's veraPDF service.
ideas.targetCustomer: Developers and maintainers of tagged-PDF generators (HTML-to-PDF pipelines, Typst and krilla users, LaTeX tagging, report and invoice generators) who want regression checks; second, small PDF-remediation vendors who promise screen-reader-tested files.
ideas.buyer: A small software team or a remediation firm, by card from its tools budget: $19 a month for one developer or $79 a month for a team with CI and batch runs; open-source projects free.
ideas.whyNow: New tagged-PDF generators in 2026 are hitting validator-pass, listener-fail faults (four GitHub issues between 2026-11-22 and 2026-11-25); pdf.js changed what its tagged layer exposes in its August and November 2026 releases; and the ADA Title II web rule's dates (2027-04-26 and 2028-04-26) keep public bodies asking for accessible PDFs.

review.findings: Wildcard review; total 20 to 16 (pain 3 to 2, willingnessToPay 3 to 2, reachability 3 to 2, competitiveGap 3 to 2). No free tool does the whole job for the same customer, so under the wildcard rule it is a rescore, not a kill. Confirmed the pdf.js and fulgur issues, accessible.org's pricing and the local capture (re-run by the reviewer). Found that the headless-Chromium capture is Chromium's reading of pdf.js's layer, not Firefox's: every struct-tree element measured zero size yet Chromium exposed the full table, so the tool would miss exactly the VoiceOver 'Table not found' case (a pdf.js bug known since Mozilla bug 1705139). The research ran an old pdf.js (5.4.394; current 6.5.438). outloud is free with a CLI, SARIF and a GitHub Actions example, and PAC 2026 is free. CommonLook tells remediators not to tune tags to one screen reader and to point readers to Acrobat Reader; WebAIM's 2026 survey puts Firefox at 15.9% of screen-reader users' main browsers. The owner's own Screen Reader Journeys and Tagging Doctor already provide the engine and veraPDF, so it should be a PDF mode of Screen Reader Journeys, re-scoped to generator developers' CI first. Dropped a Hacker News item that was praise, not a complaint, and a 2023 WebAIM post.

gateGap.closedBy: The reserve button fed by the search-ad test is the only buyer signal in the plan; the added criterion, the share of demo uploads that pass veraPDF but show a file-level heard-as fault, would show whether the pain is real for files and not only for one viewer.

ideas.wildcardReason: It builds directly on the owner's two favourite HintWise projects, Tagging Doctor's accessible tagged PDFs and Screen Reader Journeys' screen-reader transcripts, as a developer tool for accessibility. Even if it never sells alone, it is a natural PDF mode for Screen Reader Journeys.

runNotes.caveats: First run of 2026-11-26 (Thursday, small-business back-office lens; focus sources A16, B11, C10). Three provisional ideas ship, at 20, 17 and 13, and a provisional wildcard at 16; none came near the gate of 22. Twenty-four candidates were generated (18 with a small-business buyer, 8 aimed at the owner's interests); two failed a rejection rule. Six were researched: research ended one (Property Side-Ledger for MTD, free and cheap filers already serve it), and five were reviewed (four regular, one wildcard): one was killed (Year-End Books Check for QuickBooks Online, free owner-facing scanners) and four survived as rescores (Overlay Exit Check 22 to 20, Delivery Note Bill Check 18 to 17, 1099 Ready List 17 to 13, the wildcard 20 to 16). Three ideas survived after four regular reviews, so the review target was met. The 1099 Ready List ships at 13: it passes the floor (an owner's complaint dated 2026-11-20, every rejection rule), but its competitive gap is 1 and its season ends in January. Selection constraints hold: idea 3 is a Weekend MVP and ideas 1, 2 and 4 are Multi-week; ideas 1 and 2 are substantial Multi-week ideas with build plans; every regular idea has a small-business buyer (idea 1 smallBusiness true, ideas 2 and 3 Small Business Ops, which is the maximum of 2). Overlay Exit Check serves the same small Shopify shops as the published Popup Check (2026-11-03); the reviewer judged it a different problem but advises treating it as superseding Popup Check rather than shipping both, and building it, like the wildcard, as a vertical of Screen Reader Journeys. No candidate except the unreviewed Checker Second Opinion scored 19 or more, so the watchlist holds one entry. Access notes: Zendesk help centres (Hopscotch, Wave, ShootProof, Verizon Connect Work) and hhs.gov, canva.com, accountingweb.co.uk, pdfa.org, simprogroup.com and community.getjobber.com answered HTTP 403 to WebFetch; feedback.qbo.intuit.com is an empty UserVoice shell (the forum looks retired); community.shopify.com answered 429; community.squareup.com threads came back empty (HTTP 202, no body); the WebAIM discussion list has been decommissioned since 2025-08-22; developer.xero.com, developer.intuit.com and innovations.xero.com render in the browser and return no text; HMRC's software finder needs a form POST; Freelancer job pages serve a login page while the per-project API answers; the GitHub MCP issue_read tool was refused by this session's configuration (an environment fact); a testmuai.com page carried instructions aimed at AI agents and was not used.
